learningJourney.title: What is Bit Manipulation
learningJourney.explanation:
Every integer in hardware is a fixed-width vector of bits. Bit manipulation treats those bits as **64 parallel boolean lanes** or elements over $\mathbb{F}_2$, executing in single CPU cycles:

- **Test / Set / Clear / Toggle**: `(m >> i) & 1`, `m | (1 << i)`, `m & ~(1 << i)`, `m ^ (1 << i)`.
- **Lowest Set Bit (`x & -x`)**: Exploits two's complement (`-x == ~x + 1`) to isolate the least-significant 1-bit (powering Fenwick trees).
- **Kernighan's Trick (`x & (x - 1)`)**: Clears the lowest set bit (`x > 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0` tests power-of-two).
- **XOR Self-Inverse (`a ^ a == 0`)**: Finds unique non-duplicate elements in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Bitwise Alignment & Idioms (and UB pitfalls)
learningJourney.explanation:
Systems code uses bitwise math to eliminate division and pack flags into CPU cache lines (e.g., rounding `n` up to a 4,096-byte page or 64-byte cache line via `(n + align - 1) & ~(align - 1)`).

However, three language pitfalls cause subtle bugs:
1. **C/C++ Undefined Behavior**: Shifting by $\ge$ bit-width (`x << 64`) or left-shifting a negative integer is UB.
2. **32-Bit Literal Truncation**: Writing `1 << i` in Java/C++ overflows above bit 30—always write `1L << i` or `1ULL << i`.
3. **Unmasked Python `~`**: `~0b1010` yields `-11` (infinite sign extension), not `0b0101`—mask with `& ((1 << width) - 1)`.

learningJourney.title: Where Bit Manipulation is used in production systems
learningJourney.explanation: Bitwise operations power **Bloom filters**, **Roaring Bitmaps**, **memory allocators**, **network subnet masks**, and **Snowflake ID packing**.

benefits: 64-bit POPCNT and SIMD AND/OR intersect million-element sets in microseconds.
costs: Dense bitsets waste RAM on sparse IDs unless compressed into 16-bit containers (Roaring).

benefits: (n + A - 1) & ~(A - 1) aligns allocations to 64B/4KB boundaries with zero integer division.
costs: Requires alignment A to be a strict power of two.

benefits: Packs timestamp + datacenter + sequence into one 64-bit integer for lock-free generation.
costs: Bit-width limits (e.g., 41-bit timestamp) impose hard epoch/scale ceilings.

benefits: Single register, O(1) union/intersection, zero heap allocation.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which bitwise expression rounds a positive integer `n` up to the nearest multiple of a power-of-two page size `A = 4096` without division?

options.feedback: Correct: adding A - 1 pushes any non-multiple into the next block, and & ~(A - 1) clears the lower log2(A) bits.
n & (A - 1) computes n % A (the remainder), not the aligned ceiling.
n | (A - 1) sets all lower bits to 1, yielding one less than the next multiple.

_recommendedProblem.title: Active-Active Multi-Master Split-Brain Recovery
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
